exchange-rates-s1.title: The price of the arl in bels

table.caption: Bels per arl at the start of each year (invented data for practice; the arl is the currency of Arland, the bel the currency of Belvia)

exchange-rates-s2.title: A bicycle shop in Arland
exchange-rates-s2.text: A bicycle shop in Arland imports bicycles from Belvia. Each bicycle costs 800 bels, and that price has not changed. Last year, 1 arl traded for 4 bels. This year, 1 arl trades for 5 bels. (Arland, Belvia and their currencies, the arl and the bel, are invented.)

items.q: Use the table. In Year 2, what is the price of one bel in arls (arls per bel)?

why.correct: The table gives bels per arl. Flip it: $\frac{1}{2.5} = 0.4$ arls per bel. One arl buys 2.5 bels, so one bel buys 0.4 of an arl.

mistakes.why: That is the price of the arl in bels, as the table gives it. The price of the bel in arls is the reciprocal: 1 / 2.5 = 0.4.

items.q: Use the table. What happened from Year 1 to Year 2?
options: The arl appreciated and the bel depreciated
The arl depreciated and the bel appreciated
Both currencies appreciated
Neither changed in value, since prices did not change

why.correct: More bels per arl: the arl appreciated and the bel depreciated.
options: Right: one arl bought 2.0 bels and then 2.5 bels, so the arl buys more bels (it appreciated) and each bel buys less of an arl (it depreciated).
The quote is bels per arl, so a higher number means each arl buys more bels: the arl gained value.
When one currency buys more of the other, the other buys less of the first: one appreciates as the other depreciates.
The exchange rate itself changed, from 2.0 to 2.5 bels per arl; that is a change in the value of each currency against the other.

items.q: Use the table. In Year 3, a hotel in Belvia charges 300 bels a night. What does one night cost an Arland traveler, in arls?

why.correct: Turn the rate into arls per bel, $\frac{1}{1.6} = 0.625$, then multiply: $300 \times 0.625 = 187.5$ arls. Check the units: bels times arls per bel gives arls.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the bel price by bels per arl, which gives bels squared per arl. Divide by 1.6 (or multiply by 0.625 arls per bel) to get arls.

items.q: Use the table. A Belvian good keeps the same price in bels from Year 2 to Year 3. What happens to its price for a buyer in Arland, in arls?
options: It falls, because the arl appreciated
It rises, because each arl buys fewer bels
It stays the same, because the bel price did not change
It falls, because each bel buys less of an arl

why.correct: The arl depreciated against the bel, so a bel-priced good costs more arls.
options: The arl went from 2.5 to 1.6 bels: each arl buys fewer bels, so the arl depreciated, not appreciated.
Right: the arl depreciated (2.5 to 1.6 bels per arl), so an Arland buyer needs more arls for the same bel price.
The bel price is fixed, but the arl price is the bel price times arls per bel, and that rate changed.
From Year 2 to Year 3 each bel buys more of an arl (1 / 1.6 is larger than 1 / 2.5), so the bel appreciated and the good costs more arls.

items.q: What did one bicycle cost the shop last year, in arls?

why.correct: At 4 bels per arl, one bel costs $\frac{1}{4} = 0.25$ arl, so $800 \times 0.25 = 200$ arls. Equivalently, $\frac{800}{4} = 200$.

mistakes.why: You multiplied by bels per arl. To turn bels into arls, divide by the number of bels one arl buys: 800 / 4 = 200.

items.q: What does one bicycle cost the shop this year, in arls?

why.correct: At 5 bels per arl, $\frac{800}{5} = 160$ arls: 40 arls less than last year, because each arl now buys more bels.

mistakes.why: You multiplied by bels per arl. Divide the bel price by 5 bels per arl: 800 / 5 = 160.
That is last year's cost at 4 bels per arl. This year one arl buys 5 bels.

items.q: Which describes the change in the exchange rate from last year to this year?
options: The arl depreciated against the bel
The bel appreciated against the arl
The arl appreciated against the bel
Neither, because the bicycle price in bels did not change

why.correct: From 4 to 5 bels per arl: the arl appreciated, the bel depreciated.
options: One arl now buys 5 bels instead of 4, which is more, so the arl gained value against the bel.
Each bel now buys one fifth of an arl instead of one fourth, which is less, so the bel lost value.
Right: each arl buys more bels (5 instead of 4), so the arl appreciated and the bel depreciated.
The price of the good did not change, but the price of one currency in the other did.

items.q: Which person is made worse off by this change in the exchange rate, other things equal?
options: A Belvian store buying goods priced in arls
The Arland bicycle shop
An Arland family vacationing in Belvia
A Belvian who keeps savings in arls

why.correct: An appreciating arl makes arl-priced goods dearer for people paying in bels.
options: Right: each arl now costs 5 bels instead of 4, so goods priced in arls cost the Belvian store more bels.
Its bicycles now cost 160 arls instead of 200, so the change helps it.
Each of their arls buys more bels, so hotels and meals priced in bels cost them fewer arls.
Each arl saved is now worth 5 bels instead of 4, so the saver gains when the savings are counted in bels.
The interest rate a central bank pays on reserves
The price of one currency in units of another
A country's exports divided by its imports
The gap between two countries' inflation rates

why.correct: An exchange rate is the price of one currency expressed in units of another currency.
options: That is an administered interest rate of a central bank, not the price of a currency.
Right: for example, the number of dollars one euro costs, or the number of euros one dollar costs.
That ratio compares trade flows; an exchange rate is a price of money in terms of other money.
Inflation differences can move exchange rates, but an exchange rate is the price of one currency in another.

items.q: A rate quoted as arls per bel rises from 0.40 to 0.50. What happened?
options: The arl appreciated against the bel
The bel depreciated against the arl
Nothing can be said without a quote in bels per arl
The bel appreciated against the arl

why.correct: Arls per bel is the price of the bel; a higher price means the bel appreciated.
options: It now takes more arls to buy one bel, so each arl is worth less: the arl depreciated.
One bel now buys 0.50 arl instead of 0.40, which is more, so the bel gained value.
One quote is enough: the other is its reciprocal, so a rise in arls per bel is a fall in bels per arl.
Right: the quote is the price of a bel in arls, and that price rose, so the bel appreciated (and the arl depreciated).

items.q: A concert ticket in Arland costs 60 arls. The exchange rate is 1.5 bels per arl. What does the ticket cost a visitor from Belvia, in bels?

why.correct: Multiply the arl price by bels per arl: $60 \times 1.5 = 90$ bels. Units check: arls times bels per arl gives bels.

mistakes.why: You divided. Each arl costs 1.5 bels, so 60 arls cost 60 times 1.5 = 90 bels.

items.q: The arl appreciates against the bel. Which statements follow? Select all that apply.
options: The number of bels per arl rises
The bel appreciates against the arl
The number of arls per bel rises
A Belvian good with an unchanged bel price costs fewer arls
An Arland good with an unchanged arl price costs fewer bels

why.correct: An arl appreciation raises bels per arl and is the same thing as a bel depreciation; Belvian goods get cheaper in arls and Arland goods dearer in bels.
options: Right: appreciation means each arl buys more bels.
When one currency appreciates the other depreciates: each bel now buys less of an arl.
Arls per bel is the reciprocal of bels per arl, so it falls when the arl appreciates.
Right: each arl buys more bels, so the same bel price takes fewer arls.
Each arl now costs more bels, so an arl-priced good costs Belvian buyers more bels.

items.q: An Arland student pays tuition in Belvia that is fixed in bels. Which change makes the semester cheaper for the student, in arls?
options: The rate moves from 4 bels per arl to 3 bels per arl
The rate moves from 3 bels per arl to 4 bels per arl
The rate moves from 0.25 arl per bel to 0.30 arl per bel
The tuition rises in bels while the rate stays the same

why.correct: The student gains when the arl appreciates: more bels per arl.
options: Each arl buys fewer bels, so the same bel tuition costs more arls.
Right: each arl now buys more bels, so the bel tuition takes fewer arls. The arl appreciated.
Each bel now costs more arls, so the tuition costs more arls. The bel appreciated.
A higher bel price at the same rate costs more arls.

items.q: Put the steps in order to turn a price in bels into a price in arls.
options: Read the units of the quoted rate (bels per arl or arls per bel)
If the rate is in bels per arl, flip it to get arls per bel
Multiply the price in bels by arls per bel
Check that the units leave arls: bels times arls per bel gives arls

why.correct: The slip is using the rate upside down; reading the units first and checking them last catches it.

items.q: The rate moves from 2 bels per arl to 2.5 bels per arl. Student A says: "Bels per arl rose, so the arl got stronger." Student B says: "Arls per bel fell, so the bel got weaker." Who is right?
options: Student A, but Student B has the direction backward
Student B, but Student A has the direction backward
Both: they describe one change from its two sides
Neither: a higher rate means a weaker currency

why.correct: Appreciation of one currency is depreciation of the other.
options: Student B is also right: arls per bel fell from 0.5 to 0.4, so the bel buys less of an arl.
Student A is also right: each arl buys more bels, so the arl appreciated.
Right: an arl appreciation and a bel depreciation are the same change. Bels per arl rose from 2 to 2.5; arls per bel fell from 0.5 to 0.4.
In a bels-per-arl quote, a higher number means each arl buys more, so the arl is stronger.

items.q: The exchange rate moves from 2 bels per arl to 3 bels per arl. Build an answer that identifies which currency appreciated and explains how you know.

why.correct: Appreciation is about what one unit buys: each arl now buys 3 bels instead of 2.

specific.model: The arl appreciated, because each arl now buys 3 bels instead of 2, which is more bels per arl; the bel depreciated, because each bel now buys one third of an arl instead of one half.

currency.label: Which currency
options: The arl
The bel

why.1: Each bel now buys one third of an arl instead of one half, less than before, so the bel depreciated.

because.label: How you know
options: each arl now buys more bels than before
each arl now buys fewer bels than before
the number in the quote got bigger, and a bigger number is a stronger currency

why.1: From 2 to 3 bels per arl, each arl buys more bels, not fewer.
why.2: A bigger number shows appreciation only for the currency the quote is "per"; flip the quote and the number gets smaller. Give the reason: what one unit buys.

items.q: The rate is 2.5 bels per arl. A traveler from Belvia trades 1,000 bels for arls. How many arls does the traveler get?
options: 2,500 arls
400 arls
1,000 arls
250 arls
That multiplies by bels per arl. Bels divided by bels per arl gives arls: 1,000 / 2.5 = 400.
Right: each arl costs 2.5 bels, so 1,000 bels buy 1,000 / 2.5 = 400 arls.
That treats the two currencies as worth the same; the rate says one arl costs 2.5 bels.
That divides by 4, not 2.5. 1,000 / 2.5 = 400 arls.
